transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Hawthorne - Head of ML), Ethan Park (CTO), Daniel O'Neil (Security), Sofia Reyes (PM)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand model selection needs (hosted vs dedicated vs private), context-length/multilingual requirements, and tool-calling support. Customer concerned about PII, latency for live-chat flows, and budget. Agreed to send benchmarks and schedule pilot bench run.

Topics:
- Current architecture and volume
- Latency vs cost tradeoffs
- Context length requirements and retrieval use cases
- Multilingual support and tokenization concerns
- Tool-calling / function-calling for secure data access
- Security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we super appreciate the time. i'm jordan from redwood, and priya's our se, she'll go deep on perf later.
[00:12] Maya Lopez: hi, maya here. thanks, excited to dig in. quick note, we're on pacific time so timing's fine.
[00:18] Priya Shah: hey team, priya, nice to meet you. quick agenda, we'll ask a few qualification q's, run through model options, then talk deployment modes and security. sound good?
[00:27] Ethan Park: yep sounds good.
[00:29] Jordan: cool, maybe to start maya, can you walk us through current stack and workloads? token volumes, typical latency needs?
[00:36] Maya: sure. so we run a live customer support assistant and an internal analytics assistant. volume is about 120k requests / month, peak concurrency maybe 40 rps for chat, latency target for live chat is 300-500ms per response ideally, we can accept some tail up to 800ms for longer responses.
[00:54] Daniel: from security side, everything touching p-i-i needs to be controlled. we prefer bring-your-own-key and VPC for prod, but pilot can be hosted with strong data retention rules.
[01:06] Priya: good, that helps. on the model side, are you evaluating open models only or also managed models?
[01:11] Maya: open models primarily — cost is a big driver — but we need strong instruction-following, multilingual (english/spanish), and ability to do tool-calls to our backend for secure lookups.
[01:24] Jordan: makes sense. so from redwood perspective, we support hosted api (fast to get started), dedicated (reserved gpu pools), and private (vpc/on-prem). there are tradeoffs: hosted is simplest, lowest friction, but for strict KMS and VPC you'd look at private. dedicated is good middle ground for predictable throughput and cost.
[01:44] Ethan: question, how do you handle fallback if dedicated capacity is saturated? we can't have degraded experience.
[01:49] Priya: we have smart routing and fallback policies — requests can route to compatible model variants or to hosted capacity depending on policy. you can set canary/fallback rules. there is also automated cache for prefixes to reduce load.
[02:02] Maya: ok, on models, which open models would you recommend for the 300-500ms target?
[02:09] Priya: so latency depends on hardware and context length. for shorter chattish responses (<=1024 tokens), quantized 7B/13B models on A100 or similar can hit sub-500ms in dedicated setups. for more instruction-following quality and multilingual, 13B or 34B variants often balance quality. we also advise models with good tokenizer support for spanish.
[02:33] Jordan: also to call out, we have redwood-verified perf profiles for common open checkpoints; priya will share the benchmark sheet.
[02:40] Maya: great. the analytics assistant needs 8k token context frequently — retrieval augmented generation — so we need models that support 8k contexts. is that supported?
[02:48] Priya: yes, we support long-context variants. some open checkpoints have native 8k, others can be patched with efficient attention. tradeoffs: longer context increases memory and latency; we can do KV cache and prefix caching to mitigate repeated prefixes.
[03:03] Ethan: how does that interact with batching? we care about latency at 40 rps peaks.
[03:09] Priya: continuous batching in our runtime bundles tokens across requests — you can tune max batch latency. dedicated pools give you more control over batch sizes; hosted pools have sensible defaults. for 40 rps with 8k contexts, dedicated is recommended to avoid jitter.
[03:22] Daniel: data residency and keys — we need BYOK and audit logs. can you run in our VPC with our KMS?
[03:29] Jordan: yes for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and everything logs to your audit stack. for dedicated we can enable encryption-at-rest and restrict network paths but BYOK in dedicated is usually via private deployment — we can outline specifics in the security doc.
[03:43] Maya: perfect. on multilingual quality, we've seen spanish hallucinations in smaller models — any guidance?
[03:50] Priya: empirically 13B multilingual-tuned models or instruction-tuned 34B tend to perform better on spanish. you can also fine-tune or adapt via SFT on your domain prompts. we can run evals on your prompt set to quantify.
[04:04] Sofia Reyes: would you recommend managed model variants (like hosted Llama-based) vs huggingface checkpoints locally — pros/cons?
[04:11] Jordan: pros of hosted: fast onboarding, redwood handles infra, streaming, function-calling plumbing. cons: less direct KMS/BYOK for initial pilot. self-hosted or private gives control — better for regulated data. dedicated is middle for cost predictability. huggingface checkpoints give variety but need infra management.
[04:28] Ethan: tool-calling — we need secure function-calls to our inventory system without exposing PII to the model. how do you recommend?
[04:36] Priya: two patterns: one, use function-calling where the model returns structured params and your service executes the lookup; we keep all sensitive fields hashed out in the prompt; two, use a secure tool proxy — Redwood can orchestrate tool calls so raw PII never leaves your environment in private deployments. for hosted we support tool-calling but you should proxy sensitive calls through your backend and redact in-flight.
[04:58] Maya: sounds good. one of our main KPIs is cost per 1k queries; can you ballpark differences hosted vs dedicated?
[05:06] Jordan: rough rule: hosted pay-as-you-go has higher per-token unit cost but zero infra ops; dedicated reduces unit cost via reserved GPU hours and better packing, but comes with minimum commit. private has similar infra cost to dedicated plus ops. we'll send a comparative pricing sheet with example TCO.
[05:22] Maya: excellent. any concerns about model drift / regressions if we change model versions?
[05:28] Priya: we provide rollout tooling (canary, A/B) and evaluation hooks — you can tie regressions to prompt sets and get alerted. also snapshot audits of model outputs for drift detection.
[05:40] Daniel: SOC2 stuff — i need to review your audit logs and controls. do you have SOC2 or ISO reports?
[05:46] Jordan: yes, we have SOC2 type 2 and ISO27001 documents; we'll share the security pack and a short SOC2 summary. we'll also schedule a call with our security engineer if needed.
[05:57] [pause — crosstalk; someone muted/unmuted]
[06:05] Maya: ok, could you talk about tokenizer differences, especially for spanish? we saw tokenization bloat with some models which increased cost.
[06:13] Priya: great point. tokenizer choice matters; byte-level bpe vs sentencepiece can change token counts. we can run a tokenizer-demo on your sample spanish corpus to show tokenization ratios and cost impact.
[06:25] Ethan: for bench tests, what do you need from us?
[06:28] Priya: sample prompts, traffic profile (average tokens/request, peak concurrency), and any restricted fields redacted. also indicate target SLOs. we'll run bench on dedicated/hardware that matches your needs and share numbers.
[06:40] Maya: timeline — we want a pilot in Q4. is that feasible?
[06:44] Jordan: yes pilot is doable — pilot on hosted or dedicated depending on your security needs; for VPC/private it'll take longer. we can aim to have pricing and bench plan by friday and schedule a bench run next week.
[06:56] Sofia: on the topic of function-calling again, do you support multi-step tool calling and external retrieval triggers?
[07:03] Priya: yes, our runtime supports tool sequences; you can orchestrate multi-step flows and include retrieval results as context. for private deployments the orchestration can be kept entirely within your network.
[07:15] Maya: any red flags about our scale? 120k/mo seems small but our SLOs are strict.
[07:21] Jordan: at that scale we're usually able to hit your latency targets with dedicated pools and tuned batching; the larger challenges are strict BYOK + VPC which push toward private deployments but we can pilot hybrid.
[07:33] Ethan: curious about quantization: do you recommend int8 or lower for production? tradeoffs?
[07:38] Priya: int8 quant is mature for many LLMs; we also have 4-bit q options with some quality tradeoffs. we typically recommend int8 for production to preserve quality and get cost benefits; but we'll run evals to ensure no regression on your prompt set.
[07:52] Daniel: logging — what is logged on hosted? can we disable certain fields?
[07:56] Jordan: yes hosted has configurable retention and we can redact fields; private gives full control. we'll include a matrix in the security doc outlining retention, redaction, and access controls.
[08:08] Maya: want to understand multi-region routing — our customers are NA & LATAM; need low-latency for both.
[08:14] Priya: you can route by region; redwood supports regional pools and auto-fallback. for LATAM we recommend edge regions or private deployment close to your infra.
[08:26] Maya: awesome. last question — can you support on-prem if required for regulated lines of business?
[08:31] Jordan: yes, private on-prem is an option; it's the longest lead time but gives you full control over hardware, KMS, and network.
[08:39] Sofia: ok that's helpful. next steps recap?
[08:42] Jordan: recap — we'll send pricing + contract, security pack (SOC2/ISO/KMS notes), benchmark plan and spreadsheet. priya will run tokenizer sample and bench plan once you upload prompts. schedule bench for next week.
[08:56] Maya: sounds good. we'll aim to get prompts & traffic profile by nov 18.
[09:01] Jordan: perfect, thanks everyone. any final q's?
[09:04] Ethan: none from me.
[09:05] Daniel: none.
[09:06] Jordan: awesome. we'll follow up via email with the artifacts. thanks all.

[end of transcript]

Notes on transcript quality: audio to text had occasional name errors (e.g., some vendor names transcribed incorrectly) and punctuation is rough. Speaker interruptions and overlaps are kept as-is.
